title: The Importance of Being Earnest
full_review:
Alas, the importance of being honest requires advising that "The Importance of Being Earnest," a new adaptation from Miramax, is far off the mark. Oscar Wilde's bitingly witty satire of upper-class romantic silliness is reduced to a bland drawing room comedy.

Directed and adapted by Oliver Parker, he just didn't get zesty performances from either Rupert Everett or Colin Firth, who play two English gents each pretending to be named Earnest to their frivolous fiancees (Reese Witherspoon and Frances O'Conner, who fare better in bringing their characters to life).

Everett is charmless as selfish dandy Algernon and Firth's wealthy Jack is downright dull. This robs the story of heart as well as fun as each gets caught up in lies faking their first name to sweethearts who can only entertain marrying a man named Earnest.

Unfortunately, the entertaining does not extend to the audience very much. Some of Wilde's better lines have been cut from this version and the comic timing is affected. While the original play is sprightly, this film is sluggish.

Yet it starts out promisingly as Algernon plays a jazzy tune on the piano and asks his butler (a veddy British Edward Fox) what he thought of his composition. "I didn't think it was polite to listen, sir" the servant crisply replies.

Judi Dench brings some needed acidity to her role as O'Connor's imperious mother, who is not about to accept her daughter's engagement to the mysteriously orphaned Jack. And there are humorous moments in the subplot's tentative romance between spinster teacher Anna Massey and repressed rector Tom Wilkinson, but again, while Massey is goofily endearing, Wilkinson (so fine in "In the Bedroom") flounces about without making any real comedic impression.

There are visual compensations, however. The English countryside estate, lavish interior sets and richly layered Edwardian costumes provide appealing distraction until one remembers previous productions of this evergreen title that provoked continual chuckles of appreciation. In this adaptation, Parker tinkers with its timeframe; sometimes it feels more like the Roaring Twenties, yet there's a scene set in a tattoo parlor that looks really odd.

Perhaps Parker really is a "women's director." because the female actors leave their male counterparts in the dust, and Witherspoon, the movie's sole American, carries off an English accent pretty well.

Due to romantic complications and a flash of rear nudity, the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops classification is A-II -- adults and adolescents. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG -- parental guidance suggested.
